candidateRows: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent, uncaused, timeless, immaterial, and personal creator.
This is Craig's first stated reason for theism and supplies a direct cosmological inference from the universe's beginning to a personal creator.
Craig argues against an infinite past, invokes Big Bang cosmology, applies a causal principle, and infers attributes of the universe's cause.
The life-permitting fine-tuning of the universe is better explained by an intelligent cosmic designer than by atheistic chance.
Fine-tuning is one of Craig's five principal pillars and directly contrasts a designing intelligence with an accidental life-permitting universe.
Craig describes highly constrained physical constants and initial conditions, cites scientific estimates, and attributes their coordination to design.
Objective moral values exist, cannot exist without God, and therefore logically entail that God exists.
The moral argument is a distinct principal inference in Craig's cumulative case, connecting objective normativity directly to God's existence.
Craig distinguishes moral behavior and knowledge from moral ontology, argues naturalistic evolution cannot ground objective duties, and affirms objective values.
The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief support Jesus' resurrection and thus God's existence.
This is a principal component of Craig's cumulative case and connects three asserted historical facts to a divine miracle and God's existence.
Craig identifies three historical claims, maintains that naturalistic explanations fail, and infers that Jesus rose and possessed the authority he claimed.
God can be known immediately through personal experience independently of arguments for God's existence.
The experiential claim is Craig's fifth stated reason and offers an independent route to knowledge of God outside his four inferential arguments.
Craig says biblical believers encountered God directly and argues that sincere seekers may experience God without relying exclusively on external proofs.
Multiple facts can cumulatively favor naturalism over theism when each is more probable given naturalism, even without conclusively proving naturalism.
This establishes Draper's comparative-probability method and the cumulative structure governing all seven of his subsequent arguments for naturalism.
Draper uses repeated draws from differently composed jars to explain evidential likelihood and announces seven facts intended to cumulatively favor naturalism.
The absence of noticeably superior moral behavior among theists is more expected on naturalism than on theism.
This is Draper's first principal evidential comparison and applies his probability framework to the expected moral consequences of theistic belief.
Draper denies that theists are morally inferior but argues their lack of clear moral superiority is surprising if worship provides divine moral strength.
The strong dependence of consciousness and personality on brain processes favors naturalism over theism's expectation of nonphysical minds.
This is a principal component of Draper's cumulative case and contrasts naturalistic physical dependence with theistic mind-body dualism.
Draper cites correlations between mental and neural states, including personality changes from brain disease, and argues against independently existing human souls.
Evolution is more expected on naturalism than on theism because naturalism requires an evolutionary account while theism permits many creation methods.
This is one of Draper's seven principal probability comparisons and uses the differing range of available creation mechanisms to discriminate between worldviews.
Draper accepts evolution as compatible with theism but argues it is comparatively predicted by naturalism, whereas theism leaves several alternatives open.
The systematic link between pain, pleasure, and reproductive success is substantially more probable on naturalism than on theism.
This is a principal element of Draper's cumulative naturalistic case and contrasts biological functional expectations with morally governed divine purposes.
Draper argues naturalism predicts pain and pleasure serving survival and reproduction, while theism gives reason to expect their distribution to track moral purposes.
The abundance of apparently uncompensated tragedies is substantially more probable on naturalism than on theism.
This is a major evidential argument from suffering directly bearing on whether the total evidence favors naturalism rather than Christian theism.
Draper illustrates severe tragedy, argues an omnipotent God could prevent it without eliminating freedom or moral development, and compares its likelihood under the rival views.
Victims' frequent failure to experience God's comforting presence during tragedy is more expected on naturalism than on theism.
The argument adds divine hiddenness amid suffering as a distinct component of Draper's cumulative evidential case against theism.
Draper reasons that naturalism straightforwardly predicts an absence of divine comfort, whereas theism must appeal to unknown reasons for permitting sufferers to feel abandoned.
God's failure to reveal clearly which religious path and claims about Jesus are true favors naturalism over theism.
Religious disagreement and unclear revelation constitute a distinct hiddenness argument contributing directly to the cumulative comparison of naturalism and theism.
Draper notes reasonable theists disagree about Jesus and divine commands, arguing that absent clear revelation is expected if no God exists but surprising if theism is true.
Evolutionary mechanisms are too slow and cannot produce irreducibly complex systems, so evolution favors intelligent design over naturalism.
This move attempts to convert one of Draper's principal naturalistic considerations into affirmative evidence for theism and intelligent design.
Draper's claim that evolution is more expected under naturalism than under theism.

Craig argues mutation and selection operate too slowly, invokes irreducible complexity, identifies intelligent activity as the familiar explanation, and concludes sentient evolution is improbable on naturalism.
Pain and tragedy are not demonstrably improbable on Christian theism because unknown consequences and Christian doctrines can supply morally sufficient reasons.
The move supplies Craig's main cumulative reply to the evidential problem of suffering, a central consideration in the debate's overall comparison.
Draper's arguments that biologically structured pain and abundant tragedy are more probable on naturalism.

Craig argues pain supports biological continuity, distant consequences may escape human assessment, knowing God rather than happiness is life's purpose, rebellion produces evil, and eternity changes suffering's perspective.
God has clearly revealed the uniquely true religious path through Jesus' claims, miracles, and resurrection.
This directly counters Draper's religious-hiddenness argument and connects the broader theistic case to Craig's specifically Christian conclusion.
Draper's claim that conflicting religious paths show God has not clearly revealed his purposes.
Craig answers religious disagreement by appealing to Jesus' exclusive claim and its alleged authentication through miracles and resurrection, which he treats as historical evidence of revelation.
Craig's replies do not meet Draper's comparative case because evidence favors naturalism whenever it is more likely there, even if not extremely unlikely on theism.
This methodological rebuttal defends the inferential framework underlying every component of Draper's cumulative evidential case against Craig's compatibility responses.
Craig's repeated response that Draper's listed facts are not especially unlikely given Christian theism.
Draper says Craig largely asserts that the facts are not unlikely on theism, while the relevant question is whether each fact is likelier on naturalism than on theism.
Unknown goods, causal ripple effects, and eventual heavenly compensation do not provide a morally sufficient explanation for God permitting severe suffering.
This is Draper's principal rebuttal to Craig's treatment of tragedy and therefore preserves a central pillar of the naturalistic cumulative case.
Craig's claim that unknown consequences, divine purposes, and eternal life reconcile severe suffering with Christian theism.

Draper argues unknown reasons cut both ways, omnipotence removes ordinary causal constraints, and later compensation cannot retroactively provide a moral justification for inflicting or permitting suffering.
A cosmic beginning offers some support for theism, but neither establishes that the universe began nor requires a timeless cause.
The move directly evaluates and substantially limits Craig's cosmological argument, one of the principal affirmative arguments for theism in the debate.
Craig's cosmological argument that the universe began to exist and therefore must have a transcendent personal cause.
Draper cites uncertainty near the Big Bang, allows a larger eternal system, questions causation outside time, and concludes a beginning modestly favors theism without being decisive.
Objective moral truths can be necessary conceptual truths and therefore do not require God to explain their existence.
This directly rebuts the moral argument's explanatory premise while preserving moral objectivity, thereby addressing a major affirmative consideration for theism.
Craig's argument that objective moral values and duties cannot exist without God as their foundation.
Draper treats some moral propositions as necessary truths embedded in the concept of morality, comparing them to geometric truths that remain true regardless of God's existence.
An endless future is only potentially infinite, whereas an infinite past would constitute an actually completed infinite collection of events.
The distinction directly defends the temporal cosmological argument against an alleged inconsistency between rejecting an infinite past and affirming eternal life.
The objection that eternal life is inconsistent with rejecting an infinitely old universe.
In response to a question about infinity and the afterlife, Craig distinguishes completed past events from a future that continues without ever becoming actually infinite.
The goods of appreciating life or health require neither the actual quantity of suffering in the world nor a psychology dependent on suffering for contrast.
This response blocks a prominent greater-good explanation of suffering by challenging both its alleged necessity and the fixed psychological assumptions supporting it.
The suggestion that suffering is needed for human beings to cherish life as God's gift.
Draper rejects the choice between this suffering-filled world and a painless world, arguing that less suffering or altered human psychology could preserve appreciation of goods.
Vestigial anatomical structures provide explanatory evidence that humans descended from other species rather than being independently created.
The move supplies concrete empirical support for evolutionary common descent, an important component of Draper's broader naturalistic account of complex life.
The challenge that naturalism lacks a causal account of how simple organisms developed into complex human life.
Draper concedes he cannot reconstruct every mutation but argues that ear muscles and the human tailbone are naturally explained as inherited remnants from ancestral species.
Religious experience may rationally be accepted as genuine absent good defeaters, especially when it accompanies independent arguments supporting theism.
The response defends Craig's experiential case from the charge of self-induced illusion while integrating that case with his other arguments for theism.
The objection that seeking God can produce a desired but delusory religious experience.
Craig acknowledges possible delusion but argues that experiencers remain rational without contrary reasons and that his experience confirms rather than substitutes for objective considerations.
Cross-cultural moral disagreement reflects mistaken perception or differing applications of shared values rather than the absence of objective moral truths.
This move protects the moral argument's objective-value premise from a standard relativist objection grounded in historical and anthropological diversity.
The objection that divergent moral codes across societies undermine the existence of objective morality.
Craig compares moral error with perceptual error, cites plainly corrupt social judgments, and argues that apparently different customs often express common underlying values.
Objective value can arise naturally once sentient beings have preferences and welfare, because their interests can be satisfied, frustrated, benefited, or harmed.
The move answers the claim that physicalism entails nihilism by supplying a naturalistic foundation for value, wrongness, permission, and obligation.
The challenge that purely physical beings are chemical reactions without inherent value, making atheistic morality nihilistic.
Draper locates the emergence of value in conscious creatures whose preferences and welfare matter from their own perspectives, then derives moral constraints from harm and benefit.
Grounding goodness in God's nature does not explain objective value because it merely relocates the same unexplained evaluative property into God.
The argument contests the claimed explanatory advantage of theism over naturalism at the precise point where their rival accounts of moral value are compared.
The theistic contention that God explains objective moral values better than a naturalistic worldview can.
After giving a sentience-based account, Draper argues that defining God as good leaves the goodness of the divine nature unexplained and therefore adds no explanatory advantage.
Christian salvation is received through divine grace rather than earned by moral achievement, so comparative goodness does not determine admission to heaven.
The response clarifies a doctrinal premise underlying the challenge about religious outsiders, although it does not fully resolve the question of unequal exposure.
The challenge that a good non-Christian could unjustly be condemned despite living morally within another religion.
Craig rejects a merit-based picture of salvation and says transformed conduct is a consequence, while salvation itself depends on recognizing moral insufficiency and accepting grace.
Omnipotence is not limited by an inability to perform logically contradictory descriptions because such descriptions do not specify genuine tasks.
The distinction preserves the coherence of divine omnipotence against the stone paradox and supports the conceptual consistency of the theistic position.
The objection that God's inability to create and lift an unliftable stone conflicts with being all-powerful.
Craig argues that contradictions are not tasks and therefore do not constrain power; if logical impossibilities were allowed, both creating and lifting the stone would be possible.
Jesus's resurrection supports his divinity indirectly by functioning as a morally trustworthy divine confirmation of his exceptional claims and authority.
The response explains the inferential link between the resurrection and Jesus's divinity, which is essential to Craig's broader Christian evidential case.
The objection that God might resurrect Jesus without Jesus being divine, making the resurrection inconclusive.
Craig argues that a good God would not maliciously validate false claims and that the resurrection confirms Jesus's asserted authority to forgive sins and revise divine law.
